introduction: “True life is not the life of the flesh but the life of the spirit.” Bahá’u’lláh’s sentence governs these fifty-nine passages. They say that a person can be alive in body and dead in the sense that matters; that the second life is given, like water to the thirsty or a lamp lit in a niche; that it shows as joy; and that for one who has it, death is not an ending. The guide is given whole. Beside it stand fifty-nine voices from elsewhere: the Gospels and Paul on the dead who bury their dead, the Qur’an’s Light Verse and its Kawthar, the Dhammapada on the thoughtless who are “as if dead already”, Socrates, Thoreau, Wilde, Herbert, Donne. About one in five resists and ends in a question. The Preacher prefers a living dog to a dead lion, Aristotle locates the human in reason, Khayyám and Macbeth doubt that any happiness outlasts the hour, Confucius will not speak of death, and Paul warns those who think themselves alive not to boast.
questions: The readings call people “dead” who are outwardly alive. Jesus, the Dhammapada and Oscar Wilde all say something like it. What does the word point to, and how can it be used without contempt for anyone?
Miracles of raising the dead and opening blind eyes are read here as inward events. John insists that Lazarus was four days in the tomb. What do you gain and lose by each reading?
“Only when he lives in the spirit is he truly happy.” Mill says it is better to be Socrates dissatisfied. Is the life of the spirit always happy, and what kind of happiness is meant?
Wine, intoxication and ecstasy are the images several tablets choose. Why might a scripture use them, and how do Paul’s and Khayyám’s uses differ?
“The length of life has no importance.” Read Ben Jonson, the Tao Te Ching and Rabbi Jacob on the two worlds. What would it change in your plans to believe it?
The friends are told they are quickened while others are counted among the dead. Paul warns, “boast not against the branches.” How should such a sentence be received?

outside.why: “The life of the flesh is common to both men and animals.” Hamlet: what is a man, if his chief good be but to sleep and feed? A beast, no more.
Bahá’u’lláh sets the life of the flesh below a life that knows no death. The Preacher, looking only at what he can see: a living dog is better than a dead lion. What would persuade him?
A soul with the life of the spirit “bring[s] forth good fruit”. Paul lists it: love, joy, peace, longsuffering, gentleness, goodness, faith.

“Man becomes human only through spiritual life.” Aristotle gave that place to reason: the life according to reason is best, since reason more than anything else is man. Is the spiritual life something other than the life of the mind at its best?
Wisdom, service and knowledge of God make a human life. Socrates at his trial: the unexamined life is not worth living.
The life of the soul “is life”, imperishable, the radiance of grace. Jesus: I am come that they might have life, and that they might have it more abundantly.
One must not rest until “leaving behind an enduring trace in this transient world”. Longfellow’s schoolroom lines: departing, leave behind us footprints on the sands of time.
An enduring trace is to be left in a transient world. Shelley’s king left a colossal one, and the sands took it. What kind of trace does the tablet mean?
What is the spiritual life? “Characterize thyself with the characteristics of God.” Jesus: be ye therefore perfect, even as your Father which is in heaven is perfect.
The life of the spirit consists in “being quickened through the breath of the Holy Spirit”. Jesus: it is the spirit that quickeneth; the flesh profiteth nothing.
“Christ reckoned as dead those who were nonetheless outwardly and physically alive.” The saying ‘Abdu’l-Bahá has in mind.
When scripture says the blind were made to see, “the meaning of this seeing is true insight”. The man in John’s Gospel says it both ways at once: whereas I was blind, now I see.

Raising the dead is read as giving everlasting life. John tells of a man four days in the tomb and says plainly: Lazarus is dead. What is lost, and what is gained, when such a story is read only inwardly?
“Whosoever was guided aright found life.” Jesus: he that heareth my word, and believeth, is passed from death unto life.
Those without the spirit of faith “are therefore counted as dead”. The Dhammapada: those who are in earnest do not die, those who are thoughtless are as if dead already.
They have earthly life and are bereft of the other. Oscar Wilde, from another quarter altogether: to live is the rarest thing in the world. Most people exist, that is all.

Souls not vivified by the Holy Spirit “are accounted among the dead”. Terence’s line refuses to count any human being out: nothing that concerns a man is indifferent to me. How should a believer speak of those the readings call dead?
In prosperous countries “all are immersed in materialism … like a beehive”. Jesus: a man’s life consisteth not in the abundance of the things which he possesseth.
Prosperous, and heedless of eternal life. Thoreau, of his own prosperous neighbours: the mass of men lead lives of quiet desperation.
“Whoso hath not drunk, verily he is dead.” Paul uses the same figure of a life given to pleasure: dead while she liveth.
The friends are urged to drink “this heavenly Kawthar”. The word is from this chapter of the Qur’an, where it is the Abundance given to the Prophet.
This is the water “for which the divines and mystics waited”. Jeremiah on those who looked elsewhere: they have forsaken me the fountain of living waters, and hewed them out broken cisterns.
Do not deprive yourselves, “that … you may remain alive”. The Qur’an: obey God and the messenger when He calleth you to that which quickeneth you.
The fire of Thy love “quickeneth even old bones”. Ezekiel’s valley, where breath comes into the slain.
“How can we render thanks” to One who guided us when we were lost and clothed us when we were naked? The Psalm: he raiseth up the poor out of the dust.
“Through the heart-delighting fragrance you have become fresh and verdant.” George Herbert, after a long dryness: who would have thought my shrivelled heart could have recovered greenness?
“The human temple is like unto a niche, and the heart is like unto a glass globe.” ‘Abdu’l-Bahá is reading the Light Verse of the Qur’an as a picture of the believer.
“The candle of guidance is kindled within the glass of the heart” and lights every faculty. Proverbs: the spirit of man is the candle of the Lord, searching all the inward parts.
Bodily life is breath, food and water; “the spiritual life consists of the mentioning of the True One, the Love of God”. The Psalm: my soul thirsteth for God, for the living God.
“True life on this earth below consisteth in the remembrance of the Almighty.” The Qur’an: verily in the remembrance of God do hearts find rest.
The servants should “at all times … sing a new song”. The Psalm: O sing unto the Lord a new song.
At the Convention she “saw souls brought to life with the spirit of eternal life”. The first such gathering: they were all filled with the Holy Ghost.

The Cause is “like the spirit of life in this mighty body” of the world. An unknown second-century Christian said nearly the same of his own community, sojourners in every country and at home in none.
If a soul is not severed, pure and thoughtful of others, “no one can say he is a Bahá’í”. Jesus: not every one that saith unto me, Lord, Lord.
“Only when he lives in the spirit is he truly happy.” Mill, with no theology: it is better to be a human being dissatisfied than a pig satisfied. Is the higher life always the happier one?
True life is “spiritual joys and glad tidings of God”. Jesus: these things have I spoken unto you, that my joy might remain in you, and that your joy might be full.
“If you seek comfort of soul and peace of conscience, make your way to the most gracious threshold.” Augustine: our heart is restless, until it repose in Thee.
“This happiness is eternal.” Khayyám wanted a happiness he could hold: a book of verses, a jug of wine, a loaf of bread, and thou. What does each poet of happiness make of time?

One who knows he has eternal life has “a happiness which shall last throughout eternity”. Macbeth, having lost everything: life’s but a walking shadow, a tale told by an idiot, signifying nothing. What has he lost that makes life look so?
“My greatest happiness is to see you spiritually happy.” The elder in John’s letter: I have no greater joy than to hear that my children walk in truth.
“Those inebriated with the divine cup must needs experience ecstasy and joy.” At Pentecost the bystanders said, these men are full of new wine.
“Intoxicated with the wine of reunion.” The Song of Solomon: thy love is better than wine.
“I ask God to increase thy intoxication with this wine.” Paul’s contrast: be not drunk with wine; but be filled with the Spirit.
Three paths lead to spiritual happiness, and the first is “ordeals, trials and difficulties”. Jesus: strait is the gate, and narrow is the way, which leadeth unto life.
“Be lowly, that you may become noble.” Jesus: he that humbleth himself shall be exalted.
“Blessed art thou for becoming intoxicated with the cup of tribulation.” Paul: we glory in tribulations also, knowing that tribulation worketh patience.
Souls who “leave the world without having lived to the full” are a cause for grieving. Gray in the churchyard: full many a flower is born to blush unseen.
“The length of life has no importance.” Ben Jonson, on a friend dead young: in short measures life may perfect be.
“That was not death, it was life.” Donne: one short sleep past, we wake eternally, and death shall be no more.
It was not annihilation. The Qur’an of those slain in God’s way: call them not dead; nay, they are living, only ye perceive not.

‘Abdu’l-Bahá speaks with confidence of what death was for these souls. Confucius, asked about death: while you do not know life, how can you know about death? Is reticence about the next world a lack of faith?
“Lengthen your life by living according to God’s spiritual laws … This is the true longevity.” The Tao Te Ching: he who dies and yet does not perish, has longevity.

The real life is “existence in the Knowledge of God”. Rabbi Jacob weighs the two worlds both ways: one hour of good deeds here is worth more than all the life to come, and one hour there more than all of this. Why would a believer say the first half?
The souls of believers will attain “everlasting vision and eternal reunion”. Paul: then face to face; then shall I know even as also I am known.

A soul spiritually born “will have an upward journey”. Thoreau went to the woods “to live deliberately … and not, when I came to die, discover that I had not lived”. Is the fear he names the same one these readings answer?
“They are counted as among the dead; ye are quickened.” Paul to the Ephesians: you hath he quickened, who were dead in trespasses and sins.

The friends are told they are alive and others dead. Paul warns those newly grafted in: boast not against the branches; thou bearest not the root, but the root thee. How does one hear such praise safely?
The true believer’s life is “the originating purpose of all creation”. The Psalmist, under the stars, is astonished at the same thought: what is man, that thou art mindful of him?

The believer is the purpose of creation. Stephen Crane’s man tells the universe he exists and is answered that the fact creates no sense of obligation. Which of them has the evidence, and what kind of evidence could there be?

avot-one-hour-of-repentance.text: He used to say: more precious is one hour in repentance and good deeds in this world, than all the life of the world to come; And more precious is one hour of the tranquility of the world to come, than all the life of this world

thoreau-live-deliberately.text: I went to the woods because I wished to live deliberately, to front only the essential facts of life, and see if I could not learn what it had to teach, and not, when I came to die, discover that I had not lived
